Where it began

Wasim Jaffer was born in Mumbai on 16 February 1978. He piled up runs at school, including an innings of 400 not out at the age of 15, and in only his second first-class match he made 314 not out. That day he and Sulakshan Kulkarni put on 459 for the first wicket, the first time a Mumbai pair had passed 400 together, and his was the first triple-hundred for Mumbai away from home.

The player

His Test career began at home against South Africa in 2000, and facing Shaun Pollock and Allan Donald in his first series was a tough way to learn. He came back in 2002 in the West Indies, with 51 at Bridgetown and 86 in Antigua, and made a fifty at Lord's.

The best years came after his recall. His first Test hundred was exactly 100 against England at Nagpur, and in June 2006 he made 212 in Antigua over more than 500 minutes. He added hundreds against South Africa at Newlands and Bangladesh, and a second double, 202 against Pakistan at Eden Gardens in 2007. In 31 Tests from 2000 to 2008 he made 1,944 runs at 34.11, with 5 hundreds and 11 fifties, and held 27 catches.

What made him special

He was an opener with a touch of Mohammed Azharuddin about his style, and he had the patience to bat for hours on end. Nowhere was that clearer than in the Ranji Trophy. In 2011 he became its leading run-scorer, in November 2018 the first man to reach 11,000 runs in it, and in 2019 the first to play 150 matches in it. By then he had passed 19,000 first-class runs.

One-day cricket never quite took to him, and his time in that side was brief. He seemed to prefer a game that gave a man time to get going.

Away from the middle

In 2015 he moved to Vidarbha, and on 1 January 2018, when they won the Ranji Trophy against Delhi, it was Jaffer who hit the winning boundary. He spent several English summers in league cricket too, and in 2010 he set a record for runs in a season in the Huddersfield league while playing for Skelmanthorpe. He retired in March 2020 and turned to coaching, working with Bangladesh's batters and taking charge of Odisha.

And finally

His two Test wickets cost 9.00 each, an average most bowlers would envy. He was wise enough never to risk it by bowling much more.
